intro: Brighton holds the National Elm Collection, the largest surviving population of mature elms in Europe. Dutch elm disease emptied Britain of its big elms from the 1960s on. Here the Downs to the north and the sea to the south slowed the beetle down, and the council has cut infected wood out of the city's trees since the early 1970s. Four of the six trees below are elms, among them one planted around 1613 and its twin, felled in 2019 and carved into a sculpture that stands beside it.
meta_description: Brighton kept the elms Britain lost. Its National Elm Collection includes a 410-year-old English elm at Preston Park, standing beside its carved twin.
question_meta: A yew in Stanmer churchyard, over 500 years old, is Brighton's oldest tree. Where it stands, plus the elms that outlived Dutch elm disease.
question_answer: The oldest tree in Brighton is a yew on the north side of Stanmer parish church, in Stanmer Park, which Brighton and Hove City Council estimates at over 500 years old and names as the oldest tree in the city. It is 5.94 metres round, it has a slightly smaller companion yew a few steps away, and both stand in an open churchyard about twenty minutes' walk from Falmer station.
question_context: Yews resist dating. The heartwood rots away long before the rings can be counted, so an estimate rests on girth, on setting and on how the tree has been managed, and here the council and the Ancient Yew Group both settle on over 500 years for a trunk 5.94 metres round. Local tradition goes a great deal further and calls the tree Saxon, a thousand years and more. Neither body repeats that, and it is folklore rather than measurement. What is documented is how long the yews have been noticed: a drawing from around 1780 shows them, and in 1833 J.D. Parry put two curious old yew-trees in this churchyard into print. The companion measures 5.64 metres. Brighton's other candidates are elms, which is what the city is known for, and none of them comes close: the oldest, the surviving Preston Twin, was planted around 1613. Stanmer Park is a twenty to twenty-five minute walk from Falmer station through the parkland, and the churchyard sits in the old estate village at the far end, free and open in daylight.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Brighton?
faq.a: A yew on the north side of Stanmer parish church, estimated by the council at over 500 years old and measuring 5.94 metres round. Local tradition calls it Saxon and a thousand years old, which no surveyor has ever backed.

faq.q: Why does Brighton still have elms when the rest of Britain lost them?
faq.a: Geography and work. The Downs to the north and the sea to the south slow the beetles that carry Dutch elm disease, and the council has run a sanitation programme since the early 1970s, taking out infected wood tree by tree. The result is the National Elm Collection, held here since 1998.

faq.q: Are these trees free to visit?
faq.a: Yes, every one. They stand in public parks, a public garden, an open churchyard and a cemetery, with nothing to pay at any of them.

faq.q: Can I see them all in one walk?
faq.a: Not comfortably. The Royal Pavilion elm, the Queen's Park champion and the cemetery gateway elm are within a couple of kilometres of each other in central Brighton, and Preston Park is a short train ride north. Stanmer Park, with the yews and the cedars, is a separate trip out to Falmer.

trees.name: The Preston Twin

location.address: Preston Park, northern end, in front of the Walled Garden, near Preston Manor, Brighton

trees.story:
Two elms were planted here around 1613, almost certainly as part of a hedgerow, on land local accounts put under the Bishop of Chichester at the time, and grew into what Brighton and Hove City Council calls the largest and oldest surviving English elms in Europe. They had no name until Peter Bourne, the volunteer curator of the National Elm Collection, which Brighton hosts, measured them in the late 1980s and called them the Preston Twins. The eastern twin was damaged in a storm in 2017, caught Dutch elm disease the following year, and was felled in December 2019 to keep the infection off its neighbour. Its wood was carved, gilded and raised again on the same ground in spring 2023. So the north end of Preston Park holds one living elm of about 410 years and the worked remains of its twin.

The survivor is 6.38 metres round and was dedicated to Queen Elizabeth II under the Queen's Green Canopy in May 2022. It holds a colony of White-letter Hairstreak butterflies, which lay only on elm.

Dutch elm disease took the mature English elm almost everywhere else. Brighton has cut infected wood out of its elms since the early 1970s, and since 2023 it has also inoculated them against the disease, the first council in the UK to run such a programme by local account: 200 elms the first year, around 1,400 in 2025. This pair is what that buys, one still growing, one still standing, carved.
trees.how_to_recognise: One large elm at the north end of the park in front of the walled garden, with a carved and gilded trunk standing beside it.
trees.access: Free, public park, open dawn to dusk
trees.transport: Preston Park railway station, 5 min walk; also on several bus routes along London Road/Preston Drove
trees.notes: Species string normalised at write time from the research file's "English Elm (Ulmus minor 'Atinia')" to the site's canonical "English Elm (Ulmus procera)", which four live trees already use (Boston, Melbourne, New York, Portland). Same taxon under two treatments; hard rule 9 makes the common name canonical so the species page groups. Brighton's own sources use Atinia.
trees.verify_notes: 2026-10-09 outreach reply (Brighton help ask): a local correspondent offered three facts. (1) Named 'the Preston Twins' by Peter Bourne: CONFIRMED by Bourne's own 2019 Arboricultural Association article ('got their name after I measured the trees in the late 1980s'); added to the story. (2) Planted while the land belonged to the Bishop of Chichester: ADDED as a local account on Hidde's word (2026-10-09: 'volg hem'), not as our own claim. Preston Manor history (Wikipedia) has the manor passing from the bishops to the Crown by 1561, with the Shirleys holding the lease by 1613, so the c.1613 planting falls outside episcopal ownership; asked the correspondent for a source. (3) Brighton & Hove the first UK council to vaccinate elms: ADDED as 'by local account', on Hidde's word. DutchTrig was first used in the UK at Seaford in 2016 (Conservation Foundation with East Sussex CC); the council's own 2023 release makes no first-claim. The programme itself (200 elms 2023, ~1,400 in 2025) is added, sourced to the council and Brighton & Hove News. 2026-10-09 evening, Kerry Pickett: Brighton hosts the NATIONAL Elm Collection, not only the city's; story corrected.

trees.name: The Brace Elm

location.address: Royal Pavilion Garden, Brighton (sources differ on exact lawn: north, south and west edges are each named)

trees.story:
The Royal Pavilion's garden holds an elm older than the Pavilion. It was planted in 1776 and is now kept in one piece by a pair of forged iron braces clamped around a hollow stem, which is where the name comes from. Visitors have hooked padlocks onto them, the way people do to bridges, so the tree carries both the ironwork that saved it and the ironmongery it attracted.

Brighton and Hove Museums call it their oldest elm and describe it as hollow but healthy, which is the normal condition of an old elm that has got this far. The heartwood goes; the outer sleeve keeps working. The only measurements anyone has published come from a 1968 survey: 20 metres tall, 4.6 metres round, two large cavities recorded at the time and nothing since.

It is still being looked after. In March 2025 the museums took out a dead sycamore nearby, partly so that this tree would get more light.

One thing to know before you go. The sources put it on different lawns. The museums place it near the Indian Gate at the south entrance, another of their own articles calls it the West Lawn tree, and a Brighton elm resource says the southern edge. It is one tree, and the garden is small enough to settle the question on foot.
trees.how_to_recognise: The old elm with two iron bands bolted around its trunk and padlocks hooked onto them.
trees.transport: Brighton railway station, 15 min walk; central Brighton, many bus routes to Old Steine/North Street
trees.notes: Species string normalised at write time from the research file's "English Elm (Ulmus minor 'Atinia')" to the site's canonical "English Elm (Ulmus procera)", which four live trees already use (Boston, Melbourne, New York, Portland). Same taxon under two treatments; hard rule 9 makes the common name canonical so the species page groups. Brighton's own sources use Atinia.

trees.name: The Stanmer Churchyard Yew

location.address: Churchyard of Stanmer Parish Church, north side of the church, Stanmer Park, Brighton

trees.story:
In a city known for its elms, the oldest tree is a yew, and there are two of them. They grow together on the north side of Stanmer parish church, at the far end of Stanmer Park, and Brighton and Hove City Council names the larger one as the oldest tree in Brighton: 5.94 metres round, classed ancient, estimated at over 500 years. The Ancient Yew Group, who survey these trees for a living, record the same girth and put the companion at 5.64 metres.

Local tradition claims a great deal more, calling this one Saxon and a thousand years old or better. Neither the council nor the yew specialists repeat that, and nobody has dated the tree directly, because ancient yews hollow out and take their rings with them.

What is documented is how long the pair have been worth remarking on. A drawing in the Burrell Collection from around 1780 shows them, and in 1833 J.D. Parry put two curious old yew-trees in this churchyard into print, which puts them on the record while Stanmer was still a private estate rather than a public park. The churchyard is open, free and quiet, and the two trees are the first thing you meet on the north side of the church.
trees.how_to_recognise: Two big yews standing together on the north side of the church; this is the larger of the pair.
verified_sources: https://www.ancient-yew.org/yew_tree_database/stanmer/ (record places the two yews on the north side of the church, coordinates 50.870545, -0.10168022, about 30 m from our pin; status: Churchyard, public access)
trees.access: Free, public churchyard within Stanmer Park, generally open in daylight hours
trees.transport: Falmer railway station, 20-25 min walk through the park; bus routes to Stanmer village

photo.note: Hollow churchyard yew among gravestones, geotag 16 m, but two yews grow together here and the frame does not show which one is the larger

trees.name: The Stanmer House Cedar of Lebanon
trees.age_estimate: planted in the 18th century, roughly 250 to 300 years

location.address: Grounds behind Stanmer House, Stanmer Park, Brighton

trees.story:
Three cedars of Lebanon stand behind Stanmer House, and one of them is the tallest of its species in East Sussex on the council's own reckoning. They were planted in the eighteenth century, and the tradition here attaches them to Thomas Pelham, who built the house in the 1720s.

Cedrus libani was a status planting in English parkland: brought from the mountains of the Levant and set out in front of new country houses precisely because it did not look English. Flat-topped, dark, built in horizontal plates rather than a rounded crown. Three centuries on that is still what marks this group out from the parkland trees around them.

There used to be more. One of the original cedars came down in a storm at over 150 years old, and its timber was carved into badger sculptures that are still on the site, which is a better end than firewood.

Which of the three carries the height record is not something the sources settle. They describe the cedars as a group, and no girth or height figure has ever been published for any of them, only the designation. So the honest version is this: the tallest cedar in the county is one of these three, and if you know which, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: Three dark, flat-topped cedars standing together on the grass behind Stanmer House, their branches in horizontal layers.
trees.access: Free, public parkland grounds around Stanmer House, open during park hours
trees.transport: Falmer railway station, 20-25 min walk through the park; bus routes to Stanmer village

best_time.label: September to November: upright barrel cones that sit on the branches like eggs

trees.name: The Queen's Park Champion Wych Elm

location.address: Queen's Park, in the dog exercise area just above the playground, Brighton

trees.story:
The widest wych elm recorded in Sussex stands in a dog exercise area above a children's playground. The Tree Register of the British Isles holds it as the county champion for its species on girth, 389 centimetres when it was measured in June 2020, at a height of 23 metres.

Wych elm is the only elm truly native to Britain, which is part of why a champion specimen matters here beyond the size of it. Friends of Queen's Park, the group that surveys and writes up the park's trees, put it at about 200 years old and note what it has come through: Dutch elm disease, two world wars, and the Great Storm of 1987.

It is not alone. The same group describes several more elms in this corner of the park at 100 to 150 years and older, which is ordinary in Brighton and close to unheard of in the rest of England, where the mature elm population went in a single generation.

The champion measurement comes from that one group rather than from two independent surveys, so read 389 centimetres as their figure rather than a settled one. Anyone with a tape and four minutes can check it, and we would be glad of the number.
trees.how_to_recognise: The heaviest elm in the dog exercise area just above the playground, noticeably thicker in the trunk than the elms standing around it.
trees.transport: Brighton railway station, 25 min walk or short bus ride to Queen's Park Road; also walkable from the seafront

trees.name: The Cemetery Gateway Elm
trees.species: Elm, listed as Lombarts' Elm (Ulmus 'Lombartsii'), identification disputed

location.address: Entrance to Brighton and Preston Cemetery, Hartington Road, Brighton

trees.story:
It may be the last of its kind anywhere, and nobody is certain it is that kind at all. Brighton and Hove City Council listed this tree in 2022 as Ulmus 'Lombartsii', a cultivar raised at the Lombarts nursery in Zundert in the Netherlands around 1910 and now so rare in Europe that this one is described as possibly the only survivor. Wikipedia's page on the cultivar then undercuts the claim from the other side: the leaves match herbarium specimens closely enough, but the tree lacks the drooping branch habit that defines 'Lombartsii', so it may be some other corky-barked field elm instead. Both the rarity and the doubt rest on the same identification, which is why they arrive together.

What is not in dispute is the tree. It stands at the entrance to Brighton and Preston Cemetery on Hartington Road, beside a gothic terracotta gateway, with the thick corky ridging on its twigs and branches that gives this kind of elm its name. A matching elm once stood on the other side of the gate until Dutch elm disease took it, so the pair is now one.

Nobody has recorded an age, a girth or a height for it. If you can settle the name, we would like to hear it.
trees.how_to_recognise: The single elm at the cemetery gate on Hartington Road, beside the terracotta gothic archway, with corky ridged bark on its twigs.
trees.access: Free, public cemetery, open during daylight hours
trees.transport: Bus routes along Bear Road/Hartington Road; about 25-30 min walk from Brighton station

trees.name: The Tabletop Elm, Royal Pavilion Garden

location.address: Royal Pavilion Garden, Brighton BN1 1EE (by Brighton Museum, west lawn beside the Dome)

trees.story:
The most photographed tree in Brighton is not the oldest elm in its own garden. Both the city's 2022 elm leaflet and Brighton and Hove Museums give it the photography title, and the same garden holds the older Brace Elm, kept whole by iron bands. This one is a weeping wych elm, known locally as the tabletop elm, and the name explains itself. Its branches reach out level from the trunk and then droop, so the crown forms a flat-topped umbrella.

Its age is a small dispute. The leaflet, Great Elms of Brighton and Hove, says it was planted around the 1900s. The museums say it saw the Diamond Jubilee celebrations of 1897, which would make it a little older. So the honest band is 100 to 150 years, young by the standards of this map.

The same leaflet lists it as the East Sussex champion of its kind. Read that as the verdict of 2022, because bigger examples are said to have turned up since, and larger trees of this form are known elsewhere. Nobody has published a girth for it. The garden's own guide labels it 'Pendula', probably a difference of labelling rather than a different tree. If you have a tape and a minute, we would be glad of the number.
trees.access: Free. Royal Pavilion Garden is a public garden in the city centre; opening hours are published by Brighton & Hove Museums.
trees.transport: Brighton station, about 15 minutes on foot; buses to the Old Steine stop outside the garden.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the crown, its branches spreading level and drooping into a flat-topped umbrella. It stands on the west lawn of the Royal Pavilion Garden, beside the Dome and outside Brighton Museum.

trees.name: The Den Haag Elm, Preston Park

location.address: Coronation Garden, south-east entrance, Preston Park, Brighton BN1 6SD

trees.story:
The champion of this elm for all of Britain and Ireland is only 14 metres tall. Ulmus 'Den Haag' is a small cultivar, so the biggest one in these islands is a modest tree, and it has stood in Preston Park's Coronation Garden since 1953, when it was planted for the Queen's coronation.

What makes it worth finding is up in the crown. The 2022 leaflet Great Elms of Brighton and Hove calls it an extreme example of witch's broom, a deformity caused by a virus. The result is dense, tufted masses of twigs bunched among the ordinary branches.

The measurements are not new. The champion figures, reported on Wikipedia from the Tree Register, date from 2009, 14 metres high and 77 centimetres across. The Conservation Foundation's elm map recorded a girth of 252 centimetres in 2012. Nobody has published a dated photograph of this trunk more recently, so tell us how it looks.

The sources also differ on its spot. The elm map says the south-east entrance of the garden, and the Friends of Preston Park say the top of it. It is one short search either way. The surviving Preston Twin, planted around 1613, stands roughly 100 metres off, and a Camperdown elm with contorted branches grows in the same garden's south-west corner, so this is one stop on a short walk.
trees.access: Free. Preston Park is an open public park; the Coronation Garden is at its north end, a short walk from the surviving Preston Twin.
trees.transport: Preston Park station, a few minutes on foot; many buses along London Road.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the dense tufts of twigs, witch's broom, in a crown only 14 metres tall. It stands in Preston Park's Coronation Garden, recorded by the south-east entrance, about 100 metres from the Preston Twin.

trees.name: The Patcham Peace Yew

location.address: All Saints churchyard, Church Hill, Patcham, Brighton BN1 8YD

trees.story:
This yew was planted for a peace that did not last two years. The parish records of 1801, as quoted by the Ancient Yew Group, say the vicar set it at the west end of the church that year to celebrate the arrival in London of the preliminaries of peace, the first terms agreed with France in October 1801. Those terms became the Peace of Amiens the following spring, and Britain was back at war by May 1803. The tree has outlasted the treaty by more than two centuries.

That record is the only source for the planting, and it reaches us through the yew group's quotation of the parish book. If it holds, this is one of the rare yews whose age is a date rather than a guess, about 225 years.

The group's recorder visited in October 2011 and found a female tree, many-stemmed from a low trunk, 3.99 metres round at 30 centimetres from the ground. It is classed as notable rather than ancient, which is fair, since two centuries is young for a yew.

All Saints is a reason to come in its own right, one of the oldest churches in the city, with a doorway that may be Saxon. The churchyard is open in daylight. Nobody has published a recent dated photograph of this trunk, so if you go, tell us how the yew is doing.
trees.access: Free. All Saints churchyard is open to visitors during daylight (Ancient Yew Group lists it as public access).
trees.transport: Patcham is about 6 km north of the seafront; buses on the A23 London Road to Patcham, then 5 minutes on foot to the church.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its many stems rising from a low trunk, about four metres round near the ground. It stands at the west end of All Saints church in Patcham.
